title: How many switches untie a trefoil?
hook: Switch a crossing and its top strand goes under. How many until the knot falls open?

knows: a knot is a closed loop drawn with over and under crossings
doesNotKnow: that switching one crossing (the top strand goes under) can free a knot, because after the switch a strand lies on top at two crossings in a row and can slide off; and that on the trefoil and the figure-eight any one switch does it

misconception: To untie a knot you must undo every crossing, or find the one special crossing to switch.
objective: The learner can explain that one switch frees the trefoil whichever crossing it is, because after the switch a strand lies on top twice in a row and slides off.
keyState: Trefoil tally 3 of 3: each of the trefoil's three crossings, switched alone, gave a plain loop (milestones 'firstFree' then 'allThree'; the tally survives Reset and chip changes).

claims.text: The unknotting number of a knot is the fewest crossing switches, over all drawings of it, that turn it into a plain loop; it is 1 for the trefoil and for the figure-eight (reveal 'The fewest switches that can free a knot is its unknotting number: 1 for the trefoil, and for the figure-eight too.'; prediction answer '1').
claims.source: Fielden, Leigh and Woltering, 'Molecular Knots', Angew Chem Int Ed 2017 (PMC5582600, doi 10.1002/anie.201702531): 'unknotting number ... refers to the minimum number of crossings that have to be inverted to give the unknot from a given knot', twist knots have unknotting number 1; Sci Rep 2015 (PMC4354144, doi 10.1038/srep08928): 'The figure-eight knot, 4_1, is a twist knot having unknotting number one, as does 3_1'. Value 1 also derived: one switch frees each kit drawing (c3, brief check K9 also reads table u=1 for 3_1 and 4_1), and a knotted diagram needs at least one. Brief claim 4. 'and for the figure-eight too' is claimed context unless 4_1 was visited. Sources as named by the fact-checker (company/reviews/unknot-game/2026-10-16-fact-check.md, c6); Adams, The Knot Book, dropped (not opened). Builder-written; unverified.

claims.text: Some knots need more than one switch to become a plain loop (reveal 'Some knots need more than one.'). Example for the fact-checker, not in learner text: the (2,7) torus knot has unknotting number 3.
claims.source: PMC5582600 (Angew Chem Int Ed 2017, doi 10.1002/anie.201702531): unknotting number of the torus knot T(p,q) is (p-1)(q-1)/2, so 5_1 = T(2,5) has 2 and T(2,7) has 3; original proof Kronheimer and Mrowka, Topology 1993, 32, 773-826 (doi 10.1016/0040-9383(93)90051-v; cited there as ref 52). PMC4354144 (Sci Rep 2015, doi 10.1038/srep08928): 'The unknotting number of the 5_1 knot is two'. Sources as named by the fact-checker (company/reviews/unknot-game/2026-10-16-fact-check.md, c7); Brittenham and Hermiller, arXiv 2506.24088 (brief claim 5), dropped (not opened). recall.question: A knot drawing has 5 crossings. Switching any one of them gives a plain loop. How many switches did you need to free it?
recall.why: Any single switch frees it, so one is enough, whichever crossing you pick. No crossing is special, and you never need to undo them all.
